I work as an usher at a movie theater, and my job is to clean the theaters after the movie ends. One day, I was cleaning two theaters at the same time, Dark Phoenix and another movie. I noticed that the other movie was pretty crowded, so I wanted to clean Dark Phoenix quickly to save time. When I walked into Dark Phoenix, the credits were rolling, and there were four sets of people still there, probably waiting for an end credits scene. I've done this before without any issues, so I told them there's no end credits scene to help them leave faster. But this time, a couple got upset, yelled at me, and wanted to speak to a manager. They accused me of being rude and spoiling their experience, and also said I was shining a flashlight. I told my manager that the flashlight part wasn't true, but I didn't see a problem with telling them about the end credits. My manager apologized to the couple and gave them free passes. Then, my manager told me to stop telling people about the end credits. Now, I'm wondering if I did the right thing or if it was just a weird couple. I think about why I did it. I wanted to be efficient and help people save time. But maybe I shouldn't have told them because it upset some customers. I also wonder if it's my place to tell them that or if it's better to let them decide whether to stay or leave. I also consider the possibility that not all movies have end credits scenes, so maybe I was correct in that aspect. But the way I told them might have been the issue. Maybe I should have phrased it differently or not told them at all. I also think about the manager's reaction. They apologized to the couple and gave them free passes, which shows that the theater values customer satisfaction. My manager also told me to stop doing it, so maybe it's better to follow their instructions to avoid similar issues in the future. I also think about the broader implications. If I tell people there's no end credits scene, it might save time for cleaning, but it could also ruin the experience for some people who enjoy waiting for those scenes. It's a balance between efficiency and customer satisfaction. Maybe the best approach is to let people decide on their own or to inform them in a more polite and less intrusive way. In the end, I'm leaning towards the idea that while my intention was good, the way I handled it might have been the problem. The couple was upset, and the manager's reaction suggests that it's better to avoid such situations. So, I should probably stop telling people about the end credits to prevent similar incidents.
